final_note: You worked through A1.2 Nucleic acids — 15 guide statements.

concepts.def: The molecule in which the heritable information of an organism is stored and from which it is copied and expressed. In all living organisms the genetic material is DNA; the base sequence of DNA carries the information.

A non-cellular infectious particle consisting of genetic material inside a protein coat. Some viruses have RNA rather than DNA as their genetic material, but viruses are not considered to be living, so they are not exceptions to the rule that DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms.

The monomer of nucleic acids, made of three covalently bonded components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The pentose sugar is in the centre, with the phosphate group and the base each bonded to it. In diagrams, a circle represents the phosphate, a pentagon the pentose sugar and a rectangle the base.

A five-carbon sugar. In nucleotides the pentose is ribose (in RNA) or deoxyribose (in DNA); it is the central component of the nucleotide to which both the phosphate group and the nitrogenous base are bonded.

The acidic, negatively charged component of a nucleotide, bonded to the pentose sugar. When nucleotides are linked, the phosphate of one nucleotide is bonded to the sugar of the next, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone.

The covalent bond formed by condensation between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the pentose sugar of the next nucleotide in the same strand (also called a phosphodiester bond). It links nucleotides into a polynucleotide.

The continuous chain of alternating pentose sugars and phosphate groups, covalently bonded, that runs along each strand of DNA or RNA. Because every atom in the chain is covalently bonded, the backbone is strong; the bases project from it.

The nitrogen-containing components of nucleotides that carry the genetic code. DNA contains adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T); RNA contains adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil (U) in place of thymine.

The order of nitrogenous bases along a nucleic acid strand. Because the sugar–phosphate backbone is the same along the whole strand, it is the sequence of bases alone that forms the basis of the genetic code.

A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond with the release of a molecule of water. Nucleotides are joined into RNA (and DNA) by condensation between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the pentose sugar of the next.

A single strand of ribonucleotides linked by sugar–phosphate bonds formed by condensation. In a diagram the strand is drawn as an alternating sugar–phosphate chain with a base attached to each sugar; a molecule of n nucleotides is held together by n − 1 sugar–phosphate bonds.

The structure of DNA: two polynucleotide strands wound around each other, with their sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside and the bases pointing inwards, where each base is hydrogen-bonded to its complementary base on the other strand.

Describes the two strands of a DNA double helix, which run in opposite directions: one strand is oriented one way and the other strand the opposite way. In diagrams the strands are drawn antiparallel, with the sugars pointing in opposite directions.

The specific pairing of bases between the two strands of DNA: adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T), and guanine (G) always pairs with cytosine (C). The pairs are held together by hydrogen bonds, and the pairing is what makes the two strands complementary.

A weak, non-covalent attraction between a complementary pair of bases on opposite strands of DNA. Individually weak, hydrogen bonds are numerous along the molecule and together hold the two strands of the double helix together while allowing them to be separated when required.

The pentose sugars of RNA and DNA respectively. Deoxyribose has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose: in a sketch, the carbon at one position of the ring carries a hydrogen atom (–H) in deoxyribose where ribose carries a hydroxyl group (–OH).
DNA is usually double-stranded, contains deoxyribose and has the bases A, C, G and T. RNA is usually single-stranded, contains ribose and has the bases A, C, G and U (uracil in place of thymine).

DNA, and the RNAs of a cell: messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries a copy of a gene's base sequence to a ribosome; transfer RNA (tRNA), which carries amino acids to the ribosome; and ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which forms part of the structure of ribosomes.

A strand of DNA whose base sequence is used to direct the assembly of a new complementary strand of DNA (in replication) or of RNA (in transcription). The new strand is complementary to the template, not identical to it.

Because each base can hydrogen-bond stably only with its complementary base, a template strand determines the sequence of any strand built against it. In replication both strands act as templates, producing two identical DNA molecules; in transcription one strand acts as the template for a complementary mRNA, whose sequence is then translated.

Any of the four bases can occupy any position in a DNA strand, so a strand of n nucleotides has 4ⁿ possible sequences. Since a DNA molecule can be of any length, the number of possible sequences has no upper limit.

The ability of DNA to store an enormous amount of information with great economy: each nucleotide stores one of four possibilities in a space of less than a nanometre along the molecule, and a molecule can be of any length and any sequence.

The set of rules by which the base sequence of DNA (and of the mRNA transcribed from it) is translated into the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide: each group of three bases specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.

The same base triplets specify the same amino acids in essentially all living organisms, so a gene from one organism can be expressed correctly in another. This conservation of the code across all life forms is evidence of universal common ancestry.

The conclusion that all living organisms are descended from a single ancestral population. The genetic code is shared across all life forms although there is no chemical necessity for any particular triplet to specify a particular amino acid, which is best explained by inheritance of the code from a common ancestor.

The two ends of a nucleic acid strand, named after the carbon atoms of the pentose sugar: the 5' end has a phosphate group attached to the 5' carbon of its terminal sugar, and the 3' end has a free hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 3' carbon of its terminal sugar. In the backbone each phosphate links the 3' carbon of one sugar to the 5' carbon of the next.

Nucleotides can be added only to the free 3' hydroxyl group of a growing strand, so DNA and RNA are synthesized in the 5' to 3' direction. The template strand is therefore read in the 3' to 5' direction, and mRNA is translated by the ribosome in the 5' to 3' direction.
A nitrogenous base with a two-ring structure. Adenine and guanine are purines. In DNA a purine on one strand is always paired with a pyrimidine on the other.

A nitrogenous base with a single-ring structure. Cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines. Because every base pair in DNA is one purine bonded to one pyrimidine, A–T and C–G pairs have equal length, so the helix has the same three-dimensional structure regardless of the base sequence.

The basic unit of DNA packaging in eukaryotes: a length of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, held in place by an additional histone protein that is attached to the linker DNA where the DNA enters and leaves the core.

A protein around which DNA is wound in eukaryotic chromosomes. Eight histone proteins form the core of a nucleosome, with the DNA wrapped around the outside of the core; an additional histone attached to the linker DNA holds the DNA in place.
The stretch of DNA between one nucleosome core and the next. An additional histone protein attached to the linker DNA holds the DNA on the core of the nucleosome.

An experiment (1952) using bacteriophages, which consist only of DNA and protein, to find which of the two enters a bacterium and directs the production of new viruses. Phage DNA was labelled with radioactive phosphorus (³²P) and phage protein with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S); after infection and separation, the ³²P was found inside the bacteria and the ³⁵S outside, supporting the conclusion that DNA is the genetic material.

A virus that infects bacteria. The phage used by Hershey and Chase is made only of DNA enclosed in a protein coat, so tracing where each component goes during infection shows which component carries the genetic information.

The use of a radioactive isotope to trace a molecule. Because DNA contains phosphorus but not sulfur, and protein contains sulfur (in some amino acids) but not phosphorus, ³²P labels only DNA and ³⁵S labels only protein. The availability of radioisotopes as research tools is what made the Hershey–Chase experiment possible.

Measurements of the relative amounts of the four bases in DNA from diverse organisms. They showed that in every organism the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine and the amount of guanine equals the amount of cytosine (so purines equal pyrimidines), but that the proportions of A–T and G–C differ between organisms.

The earlier hypothesis that DNA was a simple repeating sequence of the four nucleotides, which would make all four bases equally abundant in every organism. Chargaff's data, showing unequal base composition that varies between species, falsified this hypothesis.

concepts.term: Problem of induction and certainty of falsification
concepts.def: No number of confirming observations can prove a general hypothesis true (the problem of induction), but a single reliable observation that contradicts the hypothesis can show it to be false (the certainty of falsification). Chargaff's data falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis in this way.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the genetic material of organisms is correct?
options: Every living organism, from bacteria to humans, uses DNA as its genetic material.
Some living organisms use RNA in place of DNA as their genetic material.
Genetic information in cells is stored in proteins rather than in DNA.
Living organisms vary in whether their genes are made of DNA or RNA.
mcqs.specStatementText: DNA is the genetic material of every living organism
mcqs.explain: DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms. The only entities that use RNA as genetic material are certain viruses, and viruses are not considered to be living.
rationales: DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms. The only entities that use RNA as genetic material are certain viruses, and viruses are not considered to be living.
A student who counts RNA viruses as living organisms picks this. Viruses are not considered to be living, so no living organism uses RNA as its genetic material.
A student who confuses a gene with its protein product picks this. Genes are lengths of DNA; the protein is what the gene's base sequence specifies, not the store of information.
A student who has generalized from RNA viruses picks this. Every living organism uses DNA; RNA viruses do not count because viruses are not living.

mcqs.q: The influenza virus contains RNA and no DNA. Why does this not contradict the statement that DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms?
options: The statement is a generalization, and influenza is one of its known exceptions.
Viruses are not considered to be living, so the statement does not apply to them.
The virus's RNA is not genetic material; its protein coat carries the genes.
RNA is just a single strand of DNA, so the virus's genetic material still counts as DNA.
mcqs.specStatementText: DNA is the genetic material of every living organism
mcqs.explain: The statement is about living organisms. Viruses are not cells and are not considered to be living, so a virus with RNA as its genetic material is not an exception to the rule.
rationales: A student who treats the virus as a living organism picks this. The statement has no living exceptions; viruses fall outside it because they are not living.
The statement is about living organisms. Viruses are not cells and are not considered to be living, so a virus with RNA as its genetic material is not an exception to the rule.
A student who thinks proteins carry genetic information picks this. The RNA of an influenza virus is its genetic material; the protein coat is not.
A student who thinks RNA and DNA differ only in strand number picks this. RNA differs from DNA in its sugar (ribose) and in having uracil, so it is a distinct nucleic acid, not a form of DNA.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?
options: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.
A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
A six-carbon sugar, glucose, bonded to a phosphate and to a base.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nucleotide has three parts, with the sugar in the middle
mcqs.explain: A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.
rationales: A student who uses 'base' and 'nucleotide' as synonyms picks this. The sugar and phosphate that make up the backbone are parts of each nucleotide, along with its base.
A student who reads the circle–pentagon–rectangle diagram as a chain picks this. The phosphate and the base are each bonded to the sugar; they are not bonded to each other.
A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.
A student who takes 'sugar' to mean glucose picks this. The sugar of a nucleotide is a pentose, with five carbon atoms: ribose or deoxyribose.

mcqs.q: What links one nucleotide to the next within a single strand of DNA?
options: A hydrogen bond between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.
A covalent bond between the base of one nucleotide and the base of the next one.
A bond formed by adding water between the sugar of one nucleotide and the next.
A covalent bond from the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleotides link sugar to phosphate to make a strong backbone
mcqs.explain: Sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms along the strand, forming the strong backbone of the molecule.
rationales: A student who thinks all the bonds in DNA are hydrogen bonds picks this. Within a strand the bonds are covalent; hydrogen bonds occur only between bases on opposite strands.
A student who pictures the bases as beads on a string picks this. The bases project from the backbone and are bonded only to their own sugar, not to each other.
A student who confuses hydrolysis with condensation picks this. The sugar–phosphate bond forms by condensation, which releases water; adding water breaks the bond.
Sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms along the strand, forming the strong backbone of the molecule.

mcqs.q: A solution of DNA is heated to 95 °C. The two strands separate, but each strand remains a continuous, intact chain of nucleotides. Which explanation is consistent with these observations?
options: The backbone of each strand is covalently bonded, so it survives heating that breaks the weaker hydrogen bonds between the strands.
The hydrogen bonds of the backbone are stronger than the covalent bonds between strands, so only the strands come apart.
Heating breaks the covalent bonds that join the two strands, while the hydrogen bonds within each strand stay intact.
The bases along each strand are covalently bonded to one another, which holds the strand together when the pairs separate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Nucleotides link sugar to phosphate to make a strong backbone
mcqs.explain: Sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms in each strand, forming a strong backbone. The strands are linked only by hydrogen bonds, which are weak enough to be broken by heat.
rationales: Sugar–phosphate bonding makes a continuous chain of covalently bonded atoms in each strand, forming a strong backbone. The strands are linked only by hydrogen bonds, which are weak enough to be broken by heat.
A student who has the two bond types the wrong way round picks this. The backbone is covalent and the link between strands is hydrogen bonding; the observation is explained only that way round.
A student who assumes the strands are joined by covalent bonds picks this. If that were so, the strands would not separate before the backbones broke, which is the opposite of what is observed.
A student who thinks the bases link nucleotides within a strand picks this. Each base is bonded only to its own sugar; it is the sugar–phosphate backbone that keeps the strand intact.

mcqs.q: Which list names the nitrogenous bases found in DNA?
options: Adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil: four bases.
Adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine: four bases.
Adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine and uracil.
Alanine, cysteine, glycine and threonine: four bases.
mcqs.specStatementText: Four bases in each nucleic acid form the code
mcqs.explain: DNA contains four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the strand forms the basis of the genetic code.
rationales: A student who attaches uracil to the wrong nucleic acid picks this. Uracil is found in RNA, where it takes the place of thymine; DNA contains thymine.
DNA contains four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The order of these bases along the strand forms the basis of the genetic code.
A student who has pooled every base name into one list picks this. Each nucleic acid has exactly four bases; uracil is not found in DNA.

A student who blurs DNA with protein picks this: alanine, cysteine, glycine and threonine are amino acids, the monomers of protein, whose names resemble the DNA bases adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine. The bases of DNA are adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine.

mcqs.q: How is a molecule of RNA formed from nucleotides?
options: Hydrolysis reactions join nucleotides through their sugars and phosphates, taking in a water molecule each time.
Hydrogen bonds form between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next in the chain.
Condensation reactions bond the phosphate of one nucleotide to the sugar of the next, releasing water.
Condensation reactions bond the base of one nucleotide to the base of the next, releasing water.
mcqs.specStatementText: RNA is a polymer built by condensation of nucleotides
mcqs.explain: RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers. Each condensation forms a covalent sugar–phosphate bond and releases one molecule of water.
rationales: A student who has condensation and hydrolysis the wrong way round picks this. Hydrolysis breaks polymers by adding water; nucleotides are joined by condensation, which releases water.
A student who thinks hydrogen bonds are the bonds of nucleic acids picks this. The bonds linking nucleotides in a strand are covalent, formed by condensation.
RNA is a polymer formed by condensation of nucleotide monomers. Each condensation forms a covalent sugar–phosphate bond and releases one molecule of water.
A student who pictures the bases as the links in the chain picks this. Condensation occurs between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next; the bases are not joined to each other.

mcqs.q: A short RNA molecule is made by joining 20 nucleotides into a single strand. What happens to water during its formation?
options: 20 molecules of water are released, one for each nucleotide.
19 molecules of water are taken in, one to form each bond.
No water is involved, because the bonds are hydrogen bonds.
19 molecules of water are released, one per bond formed.
mcqs.specStatementText: RNA is a polymer built by condensation of nucleotides
mcqs.explain: Joining 20 nucleotides into one strand requires 19 sugar–phosphate bonds, and each bond is formed by a condensation reaction that releases one molecule of water: 19 in total.
rationales: A student who counts nucleotides instead of bonds picks this. There is one bond fewer than there are nucleotides in a linear chain, so 19 water molecules are released.
A student who thinks the joining reaction uses water picks this. Bonds between nucleotides form by condensation, which releases water; water is taken in only when bonds are hydrolysed.
A student who thinks nucleotides are linked by hydrogen bonds picks this. The links are covalent sugar–phosphate bonds, each formed by a condensation that releases water.
Joining 20 nucleotides into one strand requires 19 sugar–phosphate bonds, and each bond is formed by a condensation reaction that releases one molecule of water: 19 in total.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the structure of a DNA molecule?
options: Two antiparallel strands linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, A with T and G with C.
Two strands with identical base sequences linked by hydrogen bonds between matching bases.
Two antiparallel strands linked by covalent bonds between complementary base pairs, A–T and G–C.
Two parallel strands linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, A with T and G with C.
mcqs.specStatementText: Two antiparallel strands, paired by hydrogen bonds, make the double helix
mcqs.explain: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands of nucleotides, linked by hydrogen bonding between complementary base pairs: adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine.
rationales: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands of nucleotides, linked by hydrogen bonding between complementary base pairs: adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine.
A student who thinks the second strand duplicates the first picks this. The strands are complementary, not identical: A on one strand lies opposite T on the other, and G opposite C.
A student who reasons from the stability of DNA to strong bonding picks this. The strands are linked by hydrogen bonds; the covalent bonds are within each strand's backbone.
A student who has never given a strand a direction picks this. The two strands run in opposite directions: they are antiparallel, and diagrams of DNA should show this.

mcqs.q: Part of one strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence ATGGCA. What is the base sequence of the complementary strand at the same position?
options: ATGGCA
TACCGT
UACCGU
GCAATG
mcqs.specStatementText: Two antiparallel strands, paired by hydrogen bonds, make the double helix
mcqs.explain: Each base on one strand is paired with its complement on the other: A with T, T with A, G with C and C with G. So ATGGCA is paired with TACCGT.
rationales: A student who thinks the two strands carry the same sequence picks this. The second strand is complementary to the first, so every base is replaced by its partner.
Each base on one strand is paired with its complement on the other: A with T, T with A, G with C and C with G. So ATGGCA is paired with TACCGT.
A student who puts uracil into DNA picks this. Uracil occurs only in RNA; in the complementary DNA strand adenine pairs with thymine.
A student who pairs A with G and C with T picks this. The complementary pairs in DNA are A with T and G with C.

mcqs.q: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?
options: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: two strands, ribose, uracil.
mcqs.specStatementText: How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
mcqs.explain: DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.
rationales: A student who thinks RNA is simply one strand of DNA picks this. RNA also differs in its sugar (ribose) and in having uracil instead of thymine.
A student who has the sugars the wrong way round picks this. Deoxyribose (one oxygen fewer than ribose) is the sugar of DNA, as its name says; ribose is the sugar of RNA.
DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.
A student who draws every nucleic acid as a double helix picks this. RNA is single-stranded; the number of strands is one of the three differences between the molecules.

mcqs.q: A student sketches the ring structures of ribose and deoxyribose. Which difference should the sketch show?
options: One carbon of the deoxyribose ring has an extra –OH that ribose lacks.
The deoxyribose ring has six carbon atoms where the ribose ring has five.
The rings are identical, and the sugars differ only in which base is attached.
One carbon of the deoxyribose ring carries –H where ribose carries –OH.
mcqs.specStatementText: How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
mcqs.explain: Deoxyribose is ribose with one hydroxyl group replaced by hydrogen, so it has one fewer oxygen atom. The sketch shows –H at that carbon in deoxyribose and –OH in ribose.
rationales: A student who has not parsed 'deoxy' as 'lacking an oxygen' picks this. Deoxyribose has one fewer oxygen than ribose, not one more.
A student who thinks of sugars as six-carbon molecules picks this. Both are pentoses with five carbon atoms; they differ only in one oxygen atom.
A student who thinks the only difference between DNA and RNA is the number of strands picks this. The sugars themselves differ: deoxyribose lacks one oxygen atom that ribose has.
Deoxyribose is ribose with one hydroxyl group replaced by hydrogen, so it has one fewer oxygen atom. The sketch shows –H at that carbon in deoxyribose and –OH in ribose.

mcqs.q: How does complementary base pairing allow the genetic information in a DNA molecule to be replicated?
options: Each separated strand is a template on which free nucleotides pair by hydrogen bonding, so both new molecules keep the original sequence.
Each separated strand acts as a template on which free nucleotides pair by covalent bonding, so both new molecules carry the original sequence.
Each strand is copied directly, base for base, so the new strand is identical to the strand it was built against, preserving the sequence.
Only one strand acts as a template, because the other strand has the same base sequence and would give exactly the same product if it were copied too.
mcqs.specStatementText: Complementary pairing lets DNA be copied and expressed
mcqs.explain: Because each base can hydrogen-bond stably only with its complement, the sequence of a template strand determines the sequence of the strand built against it. Both strands serve as templates, so two identical molecules result.
rationales: Because each base can hydrogen-bond stably only with its complement, the sequence of a template strand determines the sequence of the strand built against it. Both strands serve as templates, so two identical molecules result.
A student who assumes the pairing is covalent picks this. Complementarity is based on hydrogen bonding; the covalent bonds formed during replication are those of the new backbone.
A student who thinks copying means making an identical strand picks this. The new strand is complementary to its template; the original sequence is restored only across the pair of strands.
A student who thinks the two strands are identical picks this. The strands are complementary, and both act as templates so that each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand.

mcqs.q: The template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGGA at one position. What base sequence will the mRNA transcribed from it have at that position?
options: UACGGA
AUGCCU
ATGCCT
CGUAAG
mcqs.specStatementText: Complementary pairing lets DNA be copied and expressed
mcqs.explain: RNA nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing with the template: A pairs with U, T with A, C with G and G with C. So TACGGA gives AUGCCU.
rationales: A student who thinks the mRNA copies the template's sequence picks this. The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, not identical to it.
RNA nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing with the template: A pairs with U, T with A, C with G and G with C. So TACGGA gives AUGCCU.
A student who puts thymine into RNA picks this. RNA contains uracil in place of thymine, so the base paired with template A is U.
A student who pairs A with G and C with T picks this. The complementary pairs are A with U (or T) and G with C.

mcqs.q: How many different base sequences are possible for a single DNA strand that is 10 nucleotides long?
options: 4 × 10, which is exactly 40
10⁴, which is exactly 10 000
4¹⁰, which is about 1 000 000
2¹⁰, which is exactly 1024
mcqs.specStatementText: Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
mcqs.explain: Each of the 10 positions can be any of four bases, independently of the others, so the number of possible sequences is 4 × 4 × … (10 times) = 4¹⁰ = 1 048 576.
rationales: A student who combines the two numbers by multiplying them picks this. The possibilities multiply at each position, giving 4¹⁰, not 4 × 10.
A student who puts the numbers into the wrong places in the power picks this. It is the number of bases (4) raised to the number of positions (10): 4¹⁰.
Each of the 10 positions can be any of four bases, independently of the others, so the number of possible sequences is 4 × 4 × … (10 times) = 4¹⁰ = 1 048 576.
A student who counts two kinds of base pair rather than four bases picks this. Each position on a strand can hold any of four bases, so the base is 4, not 2.

mcqs.q: The human gene for insulin was inserted into a bacterium, which then produced insulin identical to the human protein. Which conclusion does this best support, and why?
options: Humans and bacteria share the same genes, because the bacterium already carried all the information needed to make human insulin.
The bacterium adopted the human genetic code in place of its own bacterial code when the human gene was inserted.
Any organism could translate any gene, because the code we observe is the only one that is chemically possible.
The genetic code is shared by humans and bacteria, because the bacterium translated human triplets into the same amino acids.
mcqs.specStatementText: One genetic code for all life points to one common ancestor
mcqs.explain: The bacterium read the human gene's base triplets exactly as human cells do, producing the same amino acid sequence. This conservation of the genetic code across life forms is evidence of universal common ancestry.
rationales: A student who takes a universal code to mean shared sequences picks this. Bacteria have no insulin gene; the gene had to be inserted, and only the code for reading it is shared.
A student who thinks each species has its own code picks this. There is no separate human code to adopt; the same code is used by both organisms, which is why the gene worked.
A student who assumes the codon assignments are fixed by chemistry picks this. The assignments are arbitrary, so sharing them is evidence of common ancestry, not chemical necessity.

The bacterium read the human gene's base triplets exactly as human cells do, producing the same amino acid sequence. This conservation of the genetic code across life forms is evidence of universal common ancestry.

mcqs.q: What do the labels 5' and 3' refer to in a strand of DNA or RNA?
options: The carbon atoms of the pentose sugar that carry the phosphate group and the hydroxyl group.
The positions of the first and last nucleotides in the strand, counted along it from the starting end.
The names given to the two different strands that together make up the DNA double helix.
The two ends of a strand, either of which can accept new nucleotides as the strand is extended.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
mcqs.explain: The numbers name carbon atoms of the pentose: the phosphate is attached to the 5' carbon and a hydroxyl group to the 3' carbon. A strand has a 5' end and a 3' end depending on which group is free.
rationales: The numbers name carbon atoms of the pentose: the phosphate is attached to the 5' carbon and a hydroxyl group to the 3' carbon. A strand has a 5' end and a 3' end depending on which group is free.
A student who reads the numbers as positions along the sequence picks this. They are the numbers of carbon atoms in each nucleotide's sugar, not counts along the strand.
A student who has seen 5' at the left of one strand and 3' at the left of the other picks this. Every strand has both a 5' end and a 3' end; the labels name ends, not strands.
A student who thinks a strand can be extended from either end picks this. Nucleotides are added only to the 3' end, which is the reason the labels matter.

mcqs.q: During replication, in which direction is a new DNA strand synthesized, and why?
options: 3' to 5', because a nucleotide can be added only to the free phosphate on the 5' carbon of the growing strand.
5' to 3', because nucleotides can be added only to the free hydroxyl on the 3' carbon of the strand.
5' to 3', because the template strand is read in the same direction as that in which the new strand grows.
In either direction, because nucleotides can be joined to whichever end of the growing strand is free.
mcqs.specStatementText: Strands have direction: 5' to 3'
mcqs.explain: The phosphate of each incoming nucleotide bonds to the free 3' hydroxyl of the last sugar in the chain, so the strand can only grow at its 3' end: synthesis is 5' to 3'. This determines how the antiparallel template is read.
rationales: A student who has the direction reversed picks this. The incoming nucleotide's phosphate joins the free 3' hydroxyl of the chain, so growth is at the 3' end and synthesis is 5' to 3'.

The phosphate of each incoming nucleotide bonds to the free 3' hydroxyl of the last sugar in the chain, so the strand can only grow at its 3' end: synthesis is 5' to 3'. This determines how the antiparallel template is read.
A student who forgets that the new strand is antiparallel to its template picks this. Synthesis is 5' to 3', which means the template is read 3' to 5', not in the same direction.
A student who thinks a chain can grow at both ends picks this. Only the 3' end carries the free hydroxyl that can react with an incoming nucleotide's phosphate.

mcqs.q: Why does the DNA double helix have the same three-dimensional structure whatever its base sequence?
options: Purines pair with purines and pyrimidines with pyrimidines, so both bases in every pair are the same size.
G–C pairs are longer than A–T pairs, but the helix adjusts its width locally so its shape is preserved.
Every base pair is one two-ring purine with one one-ring pyrimidine, so A–T and C–G pairs are of equal length.
Every base pair is one two-ring pyrimidine with one one-ring purine, so A–T and C–G pairs have equal length.
mcqs.specStatementText: Purine with pyrimidine keeps the helix a constant width
mcqs.explain: Adenine and guanine are purines (two rings); thymine and cytosine are pyrimidines (one ring). Because each pair combines one of each, all pairs are the same length and the helix has a uniform structure, which contributes to its stability.
rationales: A student who expects 'matching' bases to be alike picks this. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine; two purines would be too wide for the helix and two pyrimidines too narrow.
A student who thinks the two kinds of pair differ in size picks this. They do not: each is one purine plus one pyrimidine and the pairs have equal length, so no adjustment is needed.

Adenine and guanine are purines (two rings); thymine and cytosine are pyrimidines (one ring). Because each pair combines one of each, all pairs are the same length and the helix has a uniform structure, which contributes to its stability.
A student who has the classes reversed picks this. Purines (A, G) have two rings and pyrimidines (C, T) one; the conclusion about equal length is right but the classification is wrong.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the structure of a nucleosome?
options: Eight histone proteins are wrapped around a length of DNA, held in place by an additional histone on linker DNA.
DNA is wrapped around a core of nine histone proteins, one of which is attached to the linker DNA between the cores.
DNA is covalently bonded to a core of eight histone proteins, with the linker DNA left free between one core and the next.
DNA is wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, held in place by an additional histone attached to linker DNA.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nucleosome: DNA wrapped around eight histones
mcqs.explain: A nucleosome is a length of DNA wound around a core of eight histone proteins. An additional histone protein, attached to the linker DNA where the DNA enters and leaves the core, holds the nucleosome together.
rationales: A student who pictures the proteins as a coating on the DNA picks this. It is the DNA that is wound around the outside of the histone core, not the histones around the DNA.
A student who adds the linker histone to the core picks this. The core is eight histones; the additional histone on the linker DNA holds the DNA in place but is not part of the core.

A student who reasons from a stable association to covalent bonding picks this. DNA is held to the histones by non-covalent attraction between its negative phosphates and the positive proteins, which allows it to be released for copying.

A nucleosome is a length of DNA wound around a core of eight histone proteins. An additional histone protein, attached to the linker DNA where the DNA enters and leaves the core, holds the nucleosome together.

mcqs.q: A student uses molecular visualization software to examine a nucleosome, colouring the DNA one colour and the proteins another. What would the student observe about the association between the DNA and the proteins?
options: The DNA lies on the outside, wound around a compact core of eight protein molecules, with its phosphate backbone against the protein surface.
The proteins lie on the outside, forming a coat around a compact loop of DNA, with the protein surfaces facing outward, away from the DNA backbone.
The DNA passes straight through the centre of the protein core, with the eight proteins arranged symmetrically around it, like a sleeve around a rod.
The DNA and the proteins share covalent bonds at many points, with the backbone of the DNA fused to the surface of the protein core.
mcqs.specStatementText: A nucleosome: DNA wrapped around eight histones
mcqs.explain: In the visualization the DNA double helix winds around the outside of the histone core, which is a compact assembly of eight histone proteins; the phosphate backbone of the DNA lies against the positively charged surface of the proteins.
rationales: In the visualization the DNA double helix winds around the outside of the histone core, which is a compact assembly of eight histone proteins; the phosphate backbone of the DNA lies against the positively charged surface of the proteins.
A student who expects histones to wrap the DNA picks this. The software shows the reverse: the DNA is the outer coil and the proteins form the core it is wound around.
A student who imagines the DNA threaded through the proteins picks this. The DNA does not pass through the core; it is wound around the outside of it.
A student who assumes the association must be covalent picks this. Visualization shows the DNA lying against the protein surface without covalent links; the attraction is between charged groups.

mcqs.q: Hershey and Chase labelled one batch of bacteriophages with radioactive phosphorus (³²P) and another with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S). Why were these two elements chosen?
options: Protein contains phosphorus but not sulfur, and DNA contains sulfur but not phosphorus, so each label marked only one component.
DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, and protein sulfur but no phosphorus, so each label marked one component.
The labels showed that the phage particles contained both DNA and protein, which was enough to identify the genetic material.
The labels identified which one of the phage's many proteins carries its genetic information into the bacterial cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
mcqs.explain: Phosphorus occurs in the phosphate groups of DNA and not in protein; sulfur occurs in some amino acids of protein and not in DNA. Each radioisotope therefore traced one component of the phage exclusively.
rationales: A student who has the labels attached to the wrong molecules picks this. DNA's phosphate groups contain phosphorus; the sulfur is in the amino acids of the protein coat.

Phosphorus occurs in the phosphate groups of DNA and not in protein; sulfur occurs in some amino acids of protein and not in DNA. Each radioisotope therefore traced one component of the phage exclusively.
A student who thinks finding DNA present is the same as finding it responsible picks this. The point of labelling was to trace which component entered the bacterium and directed new phage production.
A student who thinks genes are made of protein picks this. The experiment compared DNA with protein; it showed that DNA, not any protein, enters the cell and carries the genetic information.

mcqs.q: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, bacteria were infected with labelled phages, the mixture was agitated in a blender to remove phage coats from the bacterial surface, and then centrifuged so that the bacteria formed a pellet. Most of the ³²P was in the pellet and most of the ³⁵S was in the liquid above it, and the new phages produced by the bacteria contained ³²P. What do these results show?
options: Phage protein entered the bacteria and directed the production of new phages, while the DNA stayed outside.
The phages are composed of both DNA and protein, and both components are needed for the phage to infect a bacterium.
Phage DNA entered the bacteria and directed the production of new phages, while the phage protein coats stayed outside them.
Protein is the genetic material, because the labelled protein stayed with the intact phages rather than being used.
mcqs.specStatementText: Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
mcqs.explain: ³²P labels DNA and was found in the bacterial pellet and in the progeny phages; ³⁵S labels protein and stayed in the liquid with the detached coats. So DNA, not protein, entered the cell and carried the information for making new phages.
rationales: A student who has swapped the labels picks this. ³²P marks DNA, and it was the ³²P that entered the bacteria and appeared in the new phages; the ³⁵S-labelled protein stayed outside.
A student who reads the result as a statement about composition picks this. The experiment separated the two components and showed that only the DNA entered and was passed on to new phages.

³²P labels DNA and was found in the bacterial pellet and in the progeny phages; ³⁵S labels protein and stayed in the liquid with the detached coats. So DNA, not protein, entered the cell and carried the information for making new phages.
A student who expects genes to be protein picks this. The protein that stayed outside could not have directed production of new phages inside the bacteria; the DNA that entered did.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between technology and the Hershey–Chase experiment?
options: Hershey and Chase designed the experiment first, and radioisotope techniques were then developed specifically to carry it out.
The experiment could have been done at any earlier time; radioisotopes only made the measurements more precise.
Radioisotopes revealed which molecules the phage contained, and that was sufficient to establish the genetic material.
Radioisotopes becoming available as research tools made it possible to trace DNA and protein separately during infection.
mcqs.specStatementText: Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
mcqs.explain: When radioisotopes were made available to scientists as research tools, the experiment became possible: ³²P and ³⁵S allowed the two components of the phage to be followed separately. Technological developments can open up new possibilities for experiments.
rationales: A student who assumes ideas always precede tools picks this. Radioisotopes were already available as research tools; their availability is what opened up the possibility of the experiment.
A student who sees technology as a refinement rather than an enabler picks this. Without a way to label DNA and protein separately there was no experiment to perform, precisely or otherwise.
A student who thinks composition settles the question picks this. Phages were already known to contain DNA and protein; the radioisotopes were needed to follow where each component went.

When radioisotopes were made available to scientists as research tools, the experiment became possible: ³²P and ³⁵S allowed the two components of the phage to be followed separately. Technological developments can open up new possibilities for experiments.

mcqs.q: Chargaff measured the percentage of each base in DNA from different organisms. For human DNA he found adenine 30.9%, thymine 29.4%, guanine 19.9% and cytosine 19.8%. For the bacterium E. coli he found adenine 24.7%, thymine 23.6%, guanine 26.0% and cytosine 25.7%. Which conclusion do these data support?
options: In each organism A ≈ T and G ≈ C, but base composition differs between organisms, so DNA is not a simple repeating sequence of the bases.
All four bases are present in roughly similar amounts in both organisms, which is consistent with DNA being a simple repeating tetranucleotide.
The equal amounts of A and T and of G and C prove that DNA is a double helix in which each A is hydrogen-bonded to a T and each G is bonded to a C.
The different base compositions show that humans and bacteria must use different genetic codes to specify their proteins.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chargaff's ratios falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis
mcqs.explain: In both organisms adenine matches thymine and guanine matches cytosine (purines equal pyrimidines), yet human DNA is about 40% G + C and E. coli about 52%. A repeating tetranucleotide would give 25% of each base in every organism, so the data falsify that hypothesis.
rationales: In both organisms adenine matches thymine and guanine matches cytosine (purines equal pyrimidines), yet human DNA is about 40% G + C and E. coli about 52%. A repeating tetranucleotide would give 25% of each base in every organism, so the data falsify that hypothesis.

A student who expects 25% of each base picks this. Human DNA has about 31% adenine but only 20% guanine, and the proportions differ from those in E. coli, which a repeating tetranucleotide cannot produce.
A student who reads the later explanation back into the data picks this. Base composition alone does not reveal structure; the double helix was proposed later and accounted for these equalities.
A student who conflates the genetic code with base composition picks this. The code (which triplets specify which amino acids) is the same in both organisms; only the proportions of the bases differ.

mcqs.q: The tetranucleotide hypothesis proposed that DNA was a repeating sequence of the four bases. Which statement correctly describes the role of Chargaff's data in relation to this hypothesis?
options: The hypothesis had been proved by earlier supporting measurements, so Chargaff's data could only refine it rather than reject it.
Confirming cases cannot prove a hypothesis, but Chargaff's contrary measurements were enough to show it false.
Chargaff's data replaced the hypothesis with proof that DNA is a double helix with complementary base pairs throughout.
Chargaff's data confirmed the hypothesis, since every organism he examined had all four bases present in its DNA.
mcqs.specStatementText: Chargaff's ratios falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis
mcqs.explain: This is how the certainty of falsification addresses the problem of induction. No amount of supporting data proves a general claim, but data that contradict it, such as Chargaff's unequal base proportions, show it to be false.
rationales: A student who thinks accumulated confirmations prove a hypothesis picks this. Confirmations never prove a general hypothesis; contradicting data falsify it, and that is what Chargaff's data did.

This is how the certainty of falsification addresses the problem of induction. No amount of supporting data proves a general claim, but data that contradict it, such as Chargaff's unequal base proportions, show it to be false.

A student who credits Chargaff with the structure picks this. His data measured base composition and falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis; the double helix model came later and explained his findings.

A student who takes 'all four bases present' as equivalent to 'a repeating sequence of the four bases' picks this. The hypothesis predicts equal amounts; Chargaff found unequal, organism-specific amounts.

mcqs.q: Which statement best explains why the capacity of DNA for storing information is described as limitless?
options: Capacity is not limitless: with only four bases, DNA can store far less than a code with more symbols could.
Each position can be one of only two base pairs, but the molecule is long enough to make up for the small alphabet.
A DNA molecule can be of any length and have any base sequence, so the number of possible sequences has no upper bound.
Each nucleotide added creates four more possible sequences, so a long molecule stores a great deal.
mcqs.specStatementText: Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
mcqs.explain: Any length of DNA molecule and any base sequence is possible. The number of sequences, 4ⁿ, grows without limit as n increases, and each nucleotide stores its information in a very small space, so the capacity is enormous and economical.
rationales: A student who judges capacity by the number of symbols picks this. Capacity depends on length as well; with any length allowed, four symbols give an unlimited number of sequences.
A student who counts base pairs as two kinds picks this. Each position on a strand can hold any of four bases (A–T, T–A, G–C or C–G), so the alphabet is four, not two.

Any length of DNA molecule and any base sequence is possible. The number of sequences, 4ⁿ, grows without limit as n increases, and each nucleotide stores its information in a very small space, so the capacity is enormous and economical.
A student who thinks possibilities add rather than multiply picks this. Each added nucleotide multiplies the number of possible sequences by four; that is why 4ⁿ becomes so large so quickly.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic A1.2 Nucleic acids

specStatements.text: DNA is the genetic material of every living organism
A nucleotide has three parts, with the sugar in the middle
Nucleotides link sugar to phosphate to make a strong backbone
Four bases in each nucleic acid form the code
RNA is a polymer built by condensation of nucleotides
Two antiparallel strands, paired by hydrogen bonds, make the double helix
How DNA and RNA differ: strands, sugar, bases
Complementary pairing lets DNA be copied and expressed
Any length, any sequence: DNA's storage capacity has no limit
One genetic code for all life points to one common ancestor
Purine with pyrimidine keeps the helix a constant width
A nucleosome: DNA wrapped around eight histones
Hershey and Chase traced DNA, not protein, into bacteria
Chargaff's ratios falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis

scopeNotes.howHonoured: No SL concept, misconception or item states or asks for the number of hydrogen bonds in an A–T or G–C pair, or the relative lengths of the bases. The equal length of a purine–pyrimidine pair appears only in HL objects anchored to A1.2.12, where the guide itself introduces it.
No item asks about the geometry of the helix (turns, pitch, grooves). Antiparallel is tested as a property of the two strands; the word helix is used only as the name of the molecule's shape.

No item asks the student to recall any codon, amino-acid assignment, organism or transgenic product from memory. Where an example is used as a context (human insulin made by bacteria), all the facts of the example are supplied in the stem and the item tests only the reasoning from them.

No object names the individual histone types (H2A, H2B, H3, H4, H1), gives the number of base pairs wound around the core, or extends to higher-order chromatin structure or to the role of nucleosomes in gene regulation. The molecular-visualization skill is tested through a description in words of what the software shows (q21). The non-covalent (charge-based) nature of the DNA–histone association is stated in m38, and in the key rationale of q21, as supporting context for the visualization skill, but it is never the basis of a key; the m38-linked distractors in q20 and q21 are also wrong on structural grounds (q20 omits the additional histone; in q21 the key is the guide's own wrapped-around description).
